cards.connection: English: honest, honor — Polish cześć means both 'hello' and 'honor/respect', the same idea of greeting someone with dignity
Hindi: din (दिन) · Sanskrit: dina — both dzień and din trace to PIE *dyew- (sky, daylight); the 'day' in 'good day'
Latin: nox · English: nocturnal · Sanskrit: nakta — all from PIE *nókʷts (night); dobra-noc = good-night
Sanskrit: Veda (वेद) · Hindi: dekhna (देखना) — widzenia comes from widzieć (to see), from PIE *weid- (to see/know); the Veda is literally 'what is seen/known'

cards.example_english: Thank you very much for the help.
cards.connection: English: think, thank — dziękuję shares the root with German danken and English thank; all from PIE *tong- (to think/feel)
Sanskrit: pracch (प्रच्छ्) · Hindi: poochhna (पूछना) — both from PIE *prek- (to ask/request); proszę = 'I ask/request'

cards.example_english: Excuse me, where is the toilet?
cards.connection: English: ask — the root praszam (I ask pardon) shares PIE *prek- with English ask, Sanskrit pracch
Hindi: toh (तो) — tak and toh both function as discourse affirmatives in their languages; cousins in spirit if not in etymology
Sanskrit: na (न) · Hindi: na/nahi (न/नहीं) · English: no — all from PIE *ne (negation); one of the oldest and most universal words
English: may, might — może comes from móc (to be able), all tracing to PIE *magh- (power/ability)
English: deft — dobry (good) and English deft both trace to PIE *dʰo-bʰro- (fitting, suitable)
English: wise, wisdom — the root -um- (mind/reason) connects to PIE *h₂ewm- underlying concepts of mind and understanding
English: might, power — pomoc comes from móc (to be able), the power to assist; shares PIE *magh- with English might
Latin: vita (life) · English: vital, vivid — witaj from *żywić (to live); greeting someone by wishing them life
English: ask, bardic — bar in bardzo (very) may relate to PIE *bʰer- (to carry), carrying something to the maximum
Sanskrit: yoga (योग) · English: yoke — jak (how) traces to PIE *yug- (to join/link); yoga, yoke, and jak all ask 'by what connection?'
Sanskrit: Veda (वेद) — zobaczenia from zobaczyć (to see), same PIE *weid- root as Veda and English vision; 'until we see each other again'
Sanskrit: pracch · Hindi: poochhna — proszę from PIE *prek- (to ask); 'I ask you to accept my welcome'

cards.example_polish: — Dziękuję za pomoc. — Nie ma za co!
cards.example_english: — Thanks for the help. — Don't mention it!
cards.connection: Sanskrit: na (न) — nie (not) from universal PIE *ne negation; literally 'there is nothing for which'
Sanskrit: shru (श्रु) · Hindi: sunna (सुनना) — słucham from PIE *ḱlew- (to hear); Sanskrit śravana (hearing), Konkani aikunk, all from same root
English: one, an, any — jeden from PIE *óinos; English one, Latin unus, Greek oinos all from the same root
Sanskrit: dvi (द्वि) · Hindi: do (दो) · Marathi: don (दोन) — from PIE *dwóh₁; dwa, do, dvi, two — all unmistakably the same ancient word
Sanskrit: tri (त्रि) · Hindi: tīn (तीन) · Marathi: tīn (तीन) — from PIE *tréyes; Polish trzy, Hindi tīn, English three, Latin tres — same word across 4000 years
Sanskrit: catvāri (चत्वारि) · Hindi: cār (चार) · Marathi: cār (चार) — from PIE *kʷetwóres; cztery, cār, four, quattro — all the same PIE word
Sanskrit: pañca (पञ्च) · Hindi: pāñc (पाँच) · Marathi: pāc (पाच) — from PIE *pénkʷe; pięć, pāñc, five, penta — all descend from the same root
Sanskrit: ṣaṭ (षट्) · Hindi: chaḥ (छः) · English: six — from PIE *swéḱs; the sound shifted but the number is the same ancient word

cards.example_english: There are seven days in a week.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: sapta (सप्त) · Hindi: sāt (सात) · English: seven — from PIE *septḿ̥; siedem, sāt, seven, sept — the sacred number shared across all IE languages
Sanskrit: aṣṭa (अष्ट) · Hindi: āṭh (आठ) · Marathi: āṭh (आठ) — from PIE *oḱtō(w); osiem, āṭh, eight, octo — all the same ancient word
Sanskrit: nava (नव) · Hindi: nau (नौ) · English: nine — from PIE *h₁néwn̥; dziewięć, nau, nine, novem — all cousins from the same PIE root
Sanskrit: daśa (दश) · Hindi: das (दस) · Marathi: daha (दहा) — from PIE *déḱmt; dziesięć, das, ten, dasa — one of the clearest PIE connections in the whole deck

cards.example_english: He is a hundred years old!
cards.connection: Sanskrit: śata (शत) · Hindi: sau (सौ) · Marathi: śambhar — from PIE *ḱm̥tóm; sto, sau, hundred, cent — the same ancient hundred
English: thousand — both from Proto-Germanic/Proto-IE roots meaning 'strong hundred'; the concept of a great multitude
Hindi: śūnya (शून्य) · Arabic: ṣifr — zero reached European languages via Arabic ṣifr → Italian zefiro; the concept of mathematical zero came from India through the Arab world

Sanskrit: kṛmi (कृमि) · English: crimson, worm — czerwony comes from czerw (worm); crimson dye came from a scale insect; Sanskrit kṛmi means worm/insect. Crimson, czerwony, and kṛmi all share this 'worm-dye' origin
English: blaze, bleach — biały from PIE *bʰleyH- (to shine/gleam); the whiteness of shining light
English: char (charcoal) — czarny relates to burning/charring; English char (to burn black) shares the concept of blackness through burning
Sanskrit: nabhas (नभस्) · Hindi: nabh (नभ) — niebieski literally means 'sky-colored'; niebo (sky) from PIE *nébʰos; English nebula (cloud) shares this root
Sanskrit: hari (हरि) · English: yellow, gold — zielony from PIE *ǵʰelH- (to shine/gleam yellow-green); Sanskrit hari means green/yellow/golden; Vishnu's epithet Hari relates to this shining color
Sanskrit: hari (हरि) · English: yellow, gold — same PIE *ǵʰelH- root as green above; the ancient color word covered the gold-green spectrum

Sanskrit: nāraṅga (नारङ्ग) · Hindi: nāraṅgī (नारंगी) — the word orange traveled from Sanskrit nāraṅga → Persian nārang → Arabic nāranj → European languages; Polish and Hindi both inherited the same Sanskrit word!
English: violet — both from Latin viola (the violet flower); the color named after the flower across European languages
Hindi: gulāb (गुलाब) · English: rose — różowy from róża (rose); gulāb = gul (rose, Persian) + āb (water); all named after the rose flower
English: brown, bronze — both from the same root via Italian bronzo; the color of bronze metal became the color word
English: grey/gray — both Polish szary and English grey trace back to Proto-Germanic *grēwaz (grey); cousins via different Slavic/Germanic paths
Sanskrit: mātā (माता) · Hindi: māta/mā (माँ) · Marathi: māi (माई) · Konkani: māy — all from PIE *méh₂tēr; this is one of the oldest words in human language, unchanged for 6000 years
Sanskrit: pitā (पिता) · Hindi: pitājī (पिताजी) · Marathi: bābā — from PIE *ph₂tēr; Polish ojciec evolved from the same root as Latin pater, Sanskrit pitā, English father

cards.example_english: My brother is three years old.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: bhrātā (भ्राता) · Marathi: bhrātā · English: brother — from PIE *bʰréh₂tēr; brat, bhrātā, brother — almost unchanged across thousands of years and thousands of miles
Sanskrit: svasā (स्वसा) · English: sister — from PIE *swésōr; siostra and sister are direct cognates; Sanskrit svasā is the same ancient word

cards.example_english: My son is five years old.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: sūnu (सूनु) — from PIE *suHnús; Polish syn and Sanskrit sūnu are direct cognates; the 'sun' of the family
Sanskrit: duhitā (दुहिता) · English: daughter — from PIE *dʰugH₂tēr; Polish córka evolved from the same root via Proto-Slavic; Sanskrit duhitā literally 'the milker' (who milked the cows)

cards.example_english: My grandfather is eighty years old.
cards.connection: Hindi: dādā (दादा) · Marathi: āājobā — the syllable *dada/tata for elder male is a near-universal human sound, found in dozens of unrelated languages including Hindi dādā
Hindi: bābā (बाबा) · Sanskrit: bābā — the syllable baba/babcia for elder appears across Indo-European; Hindi bābī/dādī and Polish babcia share this universal nursing-sound origin
English: queen, gynecology · Sanskrit: jāni (जनि) — from PIE *gʷén- (woman); English queen and Greek gynē (woman) are relatives; Polish żona means 'wife/woman' from the same root
Sanskrit: manu (मनु) · Hindi: mard (manliness) — from PIE *mánu- (human/man); Manu in Hindu mythology is the first human; English man shares this root
English: child — Polish dziecko and English child both emphasize the young/tender quality; PIE root relating to birth and nurturing
English: kin, kind — rodzina from rodzić (to give birth); English kin and kind relate to birth/nature; all from PIE *ǵenh₁- (to give birth/become)
Latin: avus (grandfather) — wujek traces to the concept of elder male relative; Latin avus (grandfather) gave English uncle via avunculus
Marathi: māusī (मावशी) — the nurturing sound pattern of ciocia/mama/baba recurs across many unrelated languages as a natural early-childhood sound
French: cousin · Latin: consobrinus — English cousin and Polish kuzyn both borrowed from French, ultimately from Latin; a reminder of how French spread through European courts
English: globe, ball — głowa from PIE *gʰelH-bʰ- (round/ball shape); the head as the round ball atop the body
Sanskrit: akṣi (अक्षि) · Hindi: ākh (आँख) — from PIE *h₃ekʷ- (to see); Polish oko and Hindi ākh are both descendants; English ocular and Latin oculus share this root
Latin: auris · English: ear, aural — from PIE *h₂ews- (to hear); Polish ucho, Latin auris, English ear all from the same root
Sanskrit: nāsā (नासा) · Hindi: nāk (नाक) — from PIE *néh₂s-; Polish nos and Hindi nāk are cognates; NASA (the space agency) borrowed this root for its nostril-like rocket nozzle
Sanskrit: āsya (आस्य) · Latin: os/oris (mouth) — from PIE *h₂ews-; the opening of the face; English oral shares the Latin branch of this root
Sanskrit: danta (दन्त) · Hindi: dānt (दाँत) · Marathi: dāt (दात) — from PIE *h₃dónts; ząb, dānt, tooth, dental — all from the same ancient root; Sanskrit danta gives us English dental
English: tongue, language — from PIE *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s; Latin lingua (tongue/language), English tongue; the same word means both the organ and language in Polish and many IE languages
English: sew, suture — szyja relates to the 'seam' between head and body; PIE root *syū- (to sew/join)
English: arm · Latin: armus (shoulder) — from PIE *h₂r-mo-; Polish ramię, English arm, Latin armus all from the same root; armour was named for the arm it protected
Sanskrit: aṅka (अंक) · Hindi: aṅk — from PIE *h₃enk- (bend of arm/lap); Sanskrit aṅka means the bend/lap of the arm; related to English anchor (the bent shape)
English: nail (fingernail/toenail) — from PIE *nógh- (claw/nail/extremity); the leg as the clawed extremity; English nail and Polish noga share this ancient root
Sanskrit: hṛdaya (हृदय) · Marathi: hṛday — from PIE *ḱḗr; serce, hṛdaya, heart, cardiac — all the same ancient word; Greek kardia (cardiac) is also a cousin
Sanskrit: dvāra (द्वार) · Hindi: darvāzā — twarz from tworzyć (to create/form); dvāra means door/gateway; the face as the 'doorway' of the person
English: wool, velvet — from PIE *wĺ̥H- (fleece/fiber); English wool and Polish włosy share the concept of fine fiber; both from the same PIE root
Sanskrit: kravya (क्रव्य) · English: raw, crude — from PIE *krewh₂-; krew, kravya (raw flesh), English raw and crude all relate to the concept of living/raw matter
Sanskrit: carman (चर्मन्) · English: shear, score — from PIE *sker- (to cut/divide); skin as what you cut/separate; English score (cut marks) and scar share this root
English: burgeon — brzuch from PIE *bʰer- (to carry/swell); the belly as the swelling carrier; English burgeon (to swell/grow) shares this root
English: flat, floor — plecy from PIE *pleh₂- (flat/spread out); the back as the flat surface of the body
English: loaf · German: Laib — chleb from Proto-Germanic *hlaibaz; English loaf and German Leib share this root; bread as the universal staff of life

cards.example_english: I'll have a glass of water, please.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: udán (उदन्) · English: water, wet — from PIE *wódr̥; Sanskrit udān, English water, Polish woda — all from the same root; Marathi pāṇī evolved differently
English: milk, emulsion — from PIE *H₂melǵ- (to milk/squeeze); Polish mleko and English milk are cognates via different IE branches
Latin: ovum · English: ovum, oval — from PIE *h₂ōwyom; the rounded egg shape gave us oval, ovum; Polish jajko through a different Slavic path
English: meat — in old English, meat meant any food; both Polish mięso and English meat trace to the concept of substantial nourishment
English: ruff (a type of fish) — ryba is a Slavic word; interestingly English river comes from PIE *reyH- (to flow), and fish are the river-dwellers
English: soup · Hindi: shorba — zupa via German Suppe, all from Germanic root meaning liquid food; English sup (to eat supper) shares this root
Latin: herba · English: herb — herbata = herba thea (tea herb) in Latin; English herb and herbal share this root; Polish tea is literally 'the tea herb'

cards.example_english: I drink coffee in the morning.
cards.connection: Hindi: kahvā (क़हवा) · Arabic: qahwa — kawa directly from Arabic qahwa via Turkish kahve; Hindi kahvā is the same word; coffee united Poland and India through the Arab world
Sanskrit: pā (पा) · Hindi: pīnā (पीना) — piwo from pić (to drink), both from PIE *peh₃- (to drink); piwo is literally 'the drinkable'; Hindi pīnā (to drink) shares the same ancient root
Hindi: vain/sharab · English: wine · Latin: vinum — wino from Latin vinum, a Mediterranean loanword into all European languages; wine culture spread with the Roman empire

Sanskrit: śarkarā (शर्करा) · Hindi: śakkar (शक्कर) — the word traveled: Sanskrit śarkarā → Arabic sukkar → Italian zucchero → Polish cukier; Polish and Hindi both inherited the same Sanskrit word for sugar!
Latin: sal · English: salt, salary — from PIE *séh₂ls; Roman soldiers were paid in salt (sal), giving us salary; Polish sól and English salt are PIE cousins

Sanskrit: madhu (मधु) · Marathi: madhu · Hindi: madhu — from PIE *médʰu; miód and madhu are one of the strongest connections in the deck; Sanskrit madhu means both honey and sweet; mead (honey wine) also comes from this root
Sanskrit: medas (मेदस्) — masło from mazać (to smear); Sanskrit medas means fat/marrow; both relate to the greasy/spreadable quality
English: serum — from PIE *srew- (to flow); ser and serum both come from the watery whey that separates when making cheese; cheese is literally what remains after the serum flows away

cards.example_english: I need flour for the cake.
cards.connection: English: mill, meal — from PIE *melh₂- (to grind); Polish mąka, English meal (ground grain), and mill all from the grinding root; the millstone gave us our daily bread
Sanskrit: vrīhi (व्रीहि) · Hindi: cāwal — a remarkable journey: Sanskrit vrīhi → Dravidian → Greek óruza → Latin oryza → Italian riso → Polish ryż; the grain traveled with the trade routes
French: pomme de terre (apple of the earth) — ziemniaki = ziemia (earth) + jabłko (apple) = earth-apple; same as French pomme de terre; Polish and French independently called the potato 'earth-apple'
Hindi: ṭamāṭar · Italian: pomodoro — pomidor from Italian pomodoro (golden apple = pomo d'oro); the tomato was thought to be golden when first brought to Europe
Latin: caepulla · English: chive — cebula from Latin caepula (small onion); English chive is also a cousin from the same Latin root
English: clove (of garlic) — czosnek is Slavic; the word garlic itself is Anglo-Saxon 'spear-leek'; garlic wards off vampires in both Polish and Indian folklore
English: apple — from PIE *h₂ébōl; Polish jabłko and English apple are cousins from the same root; one of the oldest fruit words in European languages

cards.example_english: I ate a banana for breakfast.
cards.connection: Hindi: kelā (केला) · Marathi: kelā — banana entered European languages from West African via Portuguese; Hindi kelā is from a different route; a fruit that traveled the world

Sanskrit: nāraṅga (नारङ्ग) · Hindi: nāraṅgī — same as the color word; both pomarańcza and Hindi nāraṅgī trace directly back to Sanskrit nāraṅga; this fruit's name is one of the clearest India-Poland connections

cards.example_english: Carrot is good for the eyes.
cards.connection: Greek: karōton · English: carrot — both marchew and English carrot come from Greek karōton, possibly related to PIE *ker- (horn — the horn-shaped root)
English: acorn — from PIE *ker- (hard shell); English acorn (oak-corn = oak-nut) and Latin nux (nut) relate to the same concept of the hard-shelled seed
Greek: elaion · English: oil — olej from Latin oleum from Greek elaion (olive oil); English oil, Latin oliva (olive), all from Greek; the olive gave the world its word for oil
Latin: acetum · English: acid, acetic — from PIE *h₂eḱ- (sharp/pointed); ocet, English acid, and acetic acid all come from the concept of sharpness/sourness
English: grab, grip — grzyb from PIE *gʰrebʰ- (to grab/seize); mushrooms 'grip' the earth; Poles are passionate mushroom foragers — it's a national tradition
Sanskrit: śvan (श्वन्) · English: hound — pies from Slavic psъ; Sanskrit śvan (dog) and English hound both from PIE *ḱwon- (dog); Polish took a different Slavic word but the concept is universal

cards.example_english: The cat sleeps on the bed.
cards.connection: Hindi: billī (बिल्ली) — kot from Late Latin cattus; the word cat spread globally from the same source; English cat and Polish kot are direct cognates via Latin

cards.example_english: The horse is a large animal.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: aśva (अश्व) · Latin: equus · English: equine — koń is from a different Slavic root, but aśva (Sanskrit), equus (Latin), and English equine all trace to PIE *h₁eḱwos; the horse's name varies but the animal shaped all our civilizations
Sanskrit: gāu (गो) · Hindi: gāy (गाय) · Marathi: gāy — from PIE *gʷow-; krowa and Hindi gāy both go back to PIE *gʷow-; English cow and Sanskrit go are the same ancient word
Sanskrit: sū-kara (सूकर) · Hindi: sūar (सूअर) · English: swine — from PIE *sūs; świnia, swine, and Hindi sūar all trace to the same PIE root; one of the oldest domesticated animal words
Sanskrit: avi (अवि) · Latin: ovis · English: ewe — from PIE *h₂ówis; Polish owca, Latin ovis, English ewe all from the same root; one of the first domesticated animals
English: goat — from PIE *gʰaidos; Polish koza and English goat are cousins; goats were among the first animals domesticated in the Middle East
Sanskrit: kukkuṭa (कुक्कुट) · Hindi: murghī — from PIE *ker- (to cry/crow); kura from the crowing sound; Sanskrit kukkuṭa (rooster) also mimics the crow; English crow relates too

cards.example_english: The wolf is a wild animal.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: vṛka (वृक) · English: wolf · Lithuanian: vilkas — from PIE *wĺ̥kʷos; wilk, wolf, vṛka are exact cognates across thousands of miles; the wolf stalked the PIE world from India to Iceland

Sanskrit: ṛkṣa (ऋक्ष) · Greek: arktos (Arctic!) — from PIE *h₂ŕ̥tḱos; the Arctic is literally 'land of the bear'; Sanskrit ṛkṣa and Greek arktos are direct cognates; Polish niedźwiedź is a euphemism ('honey-eater') — the real word was taboo
Sanskrit: mūṣa (मूष) · Hindi: cūhā · Latin: mus · English: mouse — from PIE *mūs; mysz, English mouse, and Latin mus are all the same word; Sanskrit mūṣa is a close cousin

cards.example_english: The snake crawled through the grass.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: ahi (अहि) · Latin: anguis · English: eel — from PIE *h₂engʷʰi-; Polish wąż, Sanskrit ahi (the primeval serpent), and Latin anguis all from the same root; English eel is a cousin

cards.example_english: The bird sings in the morning.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: patatī (पतति, 'it flies') · English: feather, pen — from PIE *poth₂- (to fly); Sanskrit patati (flies), English feather, and Latin penna (feather/pen) all relate to flight

cards.example_english: The eagle is the symbol of Poland.
cards.connection: Latin: aquila · English: aquiline — from PIE *h₃er-; the White Eagle is Poland's national emblem; Latin aquila gives English aquiline; the eagle symbol unites the heraldry of Poland, India (Garuda), and Rome
English: croak, guttural — żaba is a Slavic onomatopoeic word; the frog's name in most languages mimics its sound: croak, grenouille, frog — all echo the noise
Sanskrit: bhramara (भ्रमर) · English: bee — from PIE *bʰei- (to hum/buzz); Sanskrit bhramara and English bee share the buzzing sound root; honey (miód/madhu) connects bee to Sanskrit even more deeply
Latin: vulpes · English: vulpine — lis from Slavic (the 'sly one'); Latin vulpes gives English vulpine (fox-like); the fox is universally known as the clever trickster — a Slavic folk-tale staple
English: hare — zając is Slavic; English hare from PIE *ḱeh₂ro- (grey); both the hare and rabbit are symbols of speed and trickery in folklore worldwide
Sanskrit: sūrya (सूर्य) · Hindi: sūraj (सूरज) · English: sun, solar — from PIE *sóh₂wl̥; słońce, sūrya, sun, Sol — all the same ancient word for the great light

Sanskrit: māsa (मास) · Hindi: mahīnā (महीना) — from PIE *mēns-; the moon is the measurer of months; Sanskrit māsa (month) and Polish miesiąc (month) share this root; the moon-month connection is universal

cards.example_english: There are many stars in the sky.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: tārā (तारा) · Hindi: sitāra (सितारा) · English: star, astro — from PIE *h₂stḗr; gwiazda, tārā, star — all from the same ancient root; the sitar is named for stars (sitāra = star)
Sanskrit: nabhas (नभस्) · Hindi: nabh (नभ) · English: nebula — from PIE *nébʰos (cloud/sky); niebo, nabh, and English nebula (cloud in Latin) all from the same root

Hindi: zamīn (ज़मीन) · Latin: humus · English: humble, human — from PIE *dʰéǵʰōm; English human means 'of the earth'; humble means 'close to the ground'; Hindi zamīn (land) via Persian shares the root

Sanskrit: agni (अग्नि) · Hindi: āg (आग) · English: ignite — from PIE *h₁ngʷnis; ogień and agni are direct cognates; Agni is the Hindu fire god; English ignite comes from the same root; one of the most dramatic IE connections
Sanskrit: vāta (वात) · Hindi: havā (हवा) · English: wind — from PIE *h₂wéh₁nts (blowing); vāta, wind, and wiatr all trace to the same blowing root; Vayu (वायु) is the Hindu wind god
English: dew — from PIE *dʰews- (to scatter/spray); deszcz and English dew both relate to water falling from the sky; the scattering of water droplets

Sanskrit: sneha (स्नेह) · English: snow — from PIE *snigʷʰ-; Polish śnieg and English snow are cousins; Sanskrit sneha (oiliness/love — the clinging wetness) shares the root; the same word for snow became the Sanskrit word for affection
English: ice · German: Eis — from PIE *eydʰ-; Polish lód and English ice are cognates via different PIE branches; the concept of frozen water

cards.example_english: The Tatras are mountains in Poland.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: giri (गिरि) · Hindi: pahāṛ — from PIE *gʷōreh₂; Sanskrit giri (mountain/hill) is a direct cognate of Polish góra; Girnar, Girivrajapura — many Indian place names use giri for mountain

cards.example_english: The Vistula is a river in Poland.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: rājan (राजन्) · English: right, regulate — from PIE *h₃reǵ- (to flow straight/rule); river (to run straight) and rājan (king who rules straight) share a root; rivers were the original straight paths
Latin: mare · English: marine, mere — from PIE *móri; morze, Latin mare, English marine and mere (a lake) all from the same root

cards.example_english: There are many mushrooms in the forest.
cards.connection: English: glade, clearing — las is Slavic; English forest comes from Latin foris (outside, beyond the town); forests defined the edge of civilization in both Slavic and Western European cultures
Sanskrit: dāru (दारु) · Hindi: dār (दार) — from PIE *dóru (wood/tree); drzewo and Sanskrit dāru are direct cognates; English tree, tar (from wood), and true (as solid as wood) share this root
Latin: flos · English: flower, bloom, blossom — from PIE *bʰleh₃- (to blossom); Polish kwiat and Latin flos both trace to the blossoming root; English flower is from Latin via French

Sanskrit: hima (हिम) · Hindi: himālaya — from PIE *ǵʰéyōm; zima and Sanskrit hima are direct cognates; Himalaya literally means 'abode of snow/winter' (hima + ālaya); the coldest season preserved its ancient name across 4000 miles

cards.example_polish: Lato jest moją ulubioną porą roku.
cards.connection: Latin: latus (broad/wide) — lato possibly from PIE *leh₂- (broad/expansive); summer as the broad, expansive season when the world opens up

cards.example_polish: Wiosna jest moją ulubioną porą roku.
cards.connection: English: vernal, vesper — wiosna from PIE *wes-r- (spring); Latin ver (spring) gives vernal; the season of renewal shared across IE languages

cards.example_english: I threw a stone in the water.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: aśman (अश्मन्) · English: heaven — from PIE *h₂éḱmon-; remarkably, the same PIE root gave Sanskrit aśman (stone/sky-stone/thunderbolt) and is possibly related to the word for sky/heaven; the thunderbolt was the stone from heaven
Sanskrit: dāma (दाम) · Latin: domus · English: dome, domestic — from PIE *dómos; Polish dom, English dome, Latin domus all from the same root; Hindi ghar (from Persian) took a different path

Sanskrit: dvāra (द्वार) · Hindi: darvāzā (दरवाज़ा) · Marathi: dvār — from PIE *dʰwer-; drzwi, dvāra, door — one of the most direct connections; English door and Sanskrit dvāra are cousins; Hindi darvāzā via Persian also has this root
Hindi: ākh (आँख) — okno literally means 'little eye' (from oko = eye); a window is the eye of the house; same PIE *h₃ekʷ- root as eye/ocular
English: stall, stand — stół from *stojati (to stand), PIE *steh₂-; a table is a thing that stands; English stall and stool share this root
English: cross, crisscross — krzesło from crossed legs of early chairs; the cross-legged stool was the original portable seat
English: lodge, layer — łóżko from *ložiti (to lay down); English lodge (a place to lay) and lay share the concept of the horizontal resting place
Chinese: jīng (経) via Turkic — książka from Proto-Slavic *kъniga, borrowed via Avar from Chinese jīng (a scroll/classic text); your Polish book has a Chinese ancestor
Sanskrit: pi- (to write/decorate) — długopis = długo (long) + pisać (to write) = 'long-writer'; pisać from PIE *peik'- (to write/paint/decorate); Sanskrit pi- and English picture share this root

Sanskrit: dūra (दूर) + dhvani (ध्वनि) — telefon from Greek tele (far) + phōnē (voice); Sanskrit dūra (far) + dhvani (sound) express the exact same concept; the telephone in any language is 'far-sound'

cards.example_english: I drive a car to work.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: svayam (स्वयम्) — samochód = samo (self) + chód (going) = self-moving; Sanskrit svayam-calana means self-moving; automobile means the same in Greek/Latin; the concept of self-propulsion is the same across languages
English: mist, mystery — miasto from *město (place); possibly PIE *mey- (to exchange/change); cities as places where exchange happens; the market-place as the heart of civilization
English: vault, cellar — sklep originally meant a vaulted cellar-shop; the first shops were stone-vaulted underground spaces; English vault has the same architectural concept
Greek: skholē (leisure) · English: school — szkoła from Greek skholē, which meant leisure for learning; both Polish and English borrowed this Greek idea that education requires free time
English: alley, lane — ulica from PIE *h₂ewl- (enclosed lane); English alley shares this concept of a guided path between structures

cards.example_english: I don't have a lot of money.
cards.connection: Hindi: paise (पैसे) · English: penny — from Latin denarius (Roman coin); English penny, Hindi paise, and Polish pieniądze all descend from the Roman denarius; Roman coins shaped the vocabulary of money across Eurasia
Latin: hospitalis · English: hospital, host — from PIE *gʰosti- (guest/stranger); a hospital is a place of hospitality for the sick; English host, hospice, and hotel all share this root

cards.example_english: I want to be a doctor.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: bhava (भव) · Hindi: honā (होना) · English: be, become — from PIE *bʰew- (to grow/become); Sanskrit bhava (becoming/existence) and English be share the same root with Polish być

cards.example_english: I want to have a house.
cards.connection: English: medium, medical — mieć from PIE *med- (to take care of/measure); Latin medicus (doctor), English medical all from the idea of taking care/having charge of something
Sanskrit: gṛdh (गृध्) · Hindi: chāhanā (चाहना) — from PIE *gʰed- (to desire eagerly); Sanskrit gṛdha (greedy/eager) shares this root; Hindi chāh (desire/longing) is remarkably close to chcieć

Sanskrit: Veda (वेद) · Hindi: vidyā (विद्या) — from PIE *weid- (to see/know); wiedzieć and Sanskrit Veda are direct cognates; the Vedas are literally 'knowledge/what is known'; English wise, vision, video all share this root — one of the most striking connections

Sanskrit: jñāna (ज्ञान) · Hindi: jānnā (जानना) — from PIE *ǵneh₃- (to know/recognize); znać, jānnā, English know and gnosis all from the same root; Sanskrit jñāna (wisdom) and English cognition share it too
Sanskrit: eti (एति, 'goes') · Latin: ire · English: exit, issue — from PIE *ey- (to go); Sanskrit iti (goes), Latin ire, and English exit (to go out) all share this root
Sanskrit: yāna (यान) · Hindi: yātrā (यात्रा) — from PIE *yew- (to travel/convey); jechać and Sanskrit yāna (vehicle/journey) are cognates; yātrā (pilgrimage/journey) shares this root
English: mouth — mówić from PIE *mew-; English mouth (the speaking organ) and mówić (to use the mouth to speak) share the same root
Sanskrit: śru (श्रु) · Hindi: sunanā (सुनना) — from PIE *ḱlew- (to hear); słyszeć and Sanskrit śru are cognates; Sanskrit śravaṇa (hearing/listening), the ear — the same PIE *ḱlew- root
Sanskrit: vid (विद्) · English: vision, video, wise — from PIE *weid- (to see); widzieć, Sanskrit vid (to see/know), English vision — seeing and knowing are the same act in PIE
Sanskrit: ad (अद्) · Latin: edere · English: eat, edible — from PIE *h₁ed- (to eat); jeść, Latin edere, English eat all from the same root; English edible and comestible come here too
Sanskrit: pā (पा) · Hindi: pīnā (पीना) — from PIE *peh₃- (to drink); pić and pīnā are nearly identical; piwo (beer) literally means 'the drinkable'; one of the clearest verb connections
Sanskrit: svap (स्वप्) · Hindi: sonā (सोना) — from PIE *swep- (to sleep); Sanskrit svapna (dream/sleep) and Polish spać are cognates; English soporific (sleep-inducing) also comes here

Sanskrit: sthā (स्था) · Hindi: khaṛā (खड़ा) — from PIE *steh₂- (to stand); stać, Sanskrit sthā, English stand and station all from the same root; Sanskrit sthāna (place/standing) and stupa (standing mound) share it
Sanskrit: sad (सद्) · Latin: sedere · English: sit, sedentary — from PIE *sed- (to sit); siedzieć, Sanskrit sadana (seat/sitting place), English sedentary — all from the same sitting root
Sanskrit: dā (दा) · Hindi: denā (देना) — from PIE *deh₃- (to give); dać and denā are direct cognates; Latin dare (to give), English donation, data all from the same root
Sanskrit: bhara (भर) · English: bear, fertile — from PIE *bʰer- (to carry/bear); brać, Sanskrit bharati (carries), English bear (to carry) and fertile all from the same root
Sanskrit: lobha (लोभ) · Hindi: lobh (लोभ) — from PIE *lewbʰ- (to desire); lubić (to like/love) and Sanskrit lobha (desire/greed) share the same root; liking something intensely becomes wanting it

Sanskrit: kāma (काम) — from PIE *keh₁- (to desire); kochać (to love) and Sanskrit Kāma (god of love/desire) may share this root; Kāmadeva, the Hindu Cupid, and Polish love — a beautiful possible connection

Sanskrit: manas (मनस्) · Hindi: man (मन) — from PIE *men- (mind/think); myśleć and Sanskrit manas (mind) are cognates; English mental, Hindi man (heart-mind), Polish myśl (thought) — all from the same root
Sanskrit: manas (मनस्) — rozumieć = roz- (apart) + um (mind); the um root connects to mind/wisdom; understanding as 'taking apart with the mind'
Sanskrit: uktha (उक्थ) — from PIE *h₂ewk- (to speak/pronounce); learning was originally learning to recite; Sanskrit uktha (recitation/hymn) and Polish uczyć share the vocal/learning root

cards.example_english: I work from nine to five.
cards.connection: English: pray, precarious — pracować from PIE *prek- (to ask/request); work originally meant labor done at another's request; English precarious (dependent on prayer/request) shares this root

cards.example_english: I want to buy a new book.
cards.connection: Latin: caupo · English: cheap, cope — kupić from Latin caupo (shopkeeper); English cheap originally meant 'a bargain/trade'; English cope (to manage/trade) shares this root
Sanskrit: dvāra (द्वार) · Hindi: khulnā — otworzyć from *dʰwer- (door); to open = to un-door; Sanskrit dvāra and English door share this root; opening is literally 'doing something to the door'
English: mock, make — zamknąć = za (behind) + mknąć (to speed/snap shut); the sound of clicking shut echoes in Polish, English, and many languages
Sanskrit: cit (चित्) · Hindi: cetanā (चेतना) — from PIE *kʷey- (to perceive/notice); czytać and Sanskrit cit (to perceive/be aware) share the root of paying attention; reading as conscious perception

cards.example_english: I'm writing a letter to a friend.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: piṃśati (पिंशति) · English: picture, paint — from PIE *peik'- (to paint/write/decorate); pisać, English picture, and Latin pingere (to paint) all from the same root; writing began as drawing/painting

cards.example_english: I want to pay by card.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: pṛthu (पृथु) · English: flat, floor — płacić from *płat (flat piece of metal); payment was originally a flat piece of metal; Sanskrit pṛthu (broad/flat) and English flat/floor share this root
Sanskrit: dīrgha (दीर्घ) — from PIE *dl̥H-gʰo- (long/extended); dīrgha (long/tall) and duży share the concept of extended size; English tall and long distantly relate
Sanskrit: mṛdu (मृदु) · English: mild, mild — from PIE *mel- (soft/small); Sanskrit mṛdu (soft/tender/small) and Polish mały share the concept of smallness through softness
English: deft, dab — dobry from PIE *dʰo-bʰro- (fitting/suitable); English deft (skillfully good) shares this root; a 'deft' person is literally a 'good' one
English: slow, slug — zły from PIE *slew- (slack/slow); bad as 'slow/deficient'; English sluggard and sloth relate to the original sense of failing to be good

Sanskrit: nava (नव) · Hindi: nayā (नया) · Latin: novus · English: new — from PIE *néwos; nowy, nava, new, novus — one of the most consistent words across all IE languages; Nova (new star) uses the same root
Sanskrit: sthāvira (स्थाविर) · English: stand, stable — from PIE *steh₂- (to stand firm); stary and Sanskrit sthāvira (old/established elder) share the root of 'standing firm for a long time'

Sanskrit: yuvan (युवन्) · Hindi: javān (जवान) · Latin: iuvenis · English: juvenile — from PIE *h₂yew- (young/vigorous); młody and Sanskrit yuvan are cognates; Hindi javān (young man/soldier) shares this root
English: fine, refined — piękny from *pěknъ; the concept of beauty as fineness and refinement is shared; Latin bellus (beautiful) gives English belle and beauty via French

Sanskrit: ghṛta (घृत) · Hindi: garm (गर्म) — from PIE *gʷʰer- (warm/hot); gorący and Sanskrit ghṛta (ghee/clarified butter — the heated/clarified one) share this root; ghee is literally 'the hot stuff'
Sanskrit: hima (हिम) — zimny from zima (winter); same PIE *ǵʰéyōm root as Himalaya; cold=wintry=snowy, a connected chain from Poland to the Himalayas
English: whip, sweep — szybki from *šybati (to swing/sweep); English whip (fast movement) and sweep share the concept of swift motion
Sanskrit: vara (वर) · English: will, well — wolny (both slow and free) from PIE *welH- (to will/choose); to be free is to move at your own will; Sanskrit vara (wish/boon/choice) shares this root

Sanskrit: laghu (लघु) · English: light (not heavy) — from PIE *h₁lengʷʰ- (light/nimble); łatwy and Sanskrit laghu (light/easy/quick) share the concept that what is light is easy; English light and agile come from the same root
English: trudge, tread — from PIE *trud- (to push/press); trudny and English trudge share the concept of laborious effort; difficulty as having to push through

Sanskrit: śam (शम्) · English: happy (from hap = luck) — szczęście (happiness) relates to good fortune/luck; Sanskrit śam (peace/well-being) and English happy (from lucky) both reach happiness through external good
Sanskrit: gal (गल) · English: gullet, gulp — from PIE *gel- (to swallow/devour); głodny and English gullet (throat for swallowing) share the devouring root; hunger is the urge to swallow
English: muddy, muddle — zmęczony from *mącić (to muddy/confuse); tiredness as mental muddling; English muddle (confused/tired state) shares the concept

Sanskrit: cit (चित्) · Hindi: cetanā (चेतना) — from PIE *kʷey- (to perceive/be aware); ciekawy (curious) and Sanskrit cit (consciousness/awareness) share the root of attentive perception; Caitanya (consciousness) uses this root
Sanskrit: kāla (काल) · Hindi: waqt (from Arabic) — czas may connect to PIE *kʷo- (when/how); Sanskrit kāla (time/fate/the dark one) is the Hindu god of time; the concept of time as the great force

Sanskrit: dina (दिन) · Hindi: din (दिन) — from PIE *dyew- (sky/day/light); dzień, Sanskrit dina, Hindi din — all from the sky-god root; English day, Latin dies (diary, diurnal), and Sanskrit dina all share PIE *dyew-
Sanskrit: nakta (नक्त) · Latin: nox · English: nocturnal — from PIE *nókʷts; Polish noc, English nocturnal, Latin nox all from the same root; Sanskrit nakta (night) is a direct cognate

cards.example_english: I get up at seven in the morning.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: uṣas (उषस्) · English: east, aurora — from PIE *h₂ews- (dawn); Sanskrit Uṣas (goddess of dawn), English east and Easter, Latin aurora — all from the same dawn root; rano (morning) echoes the ancient reverence for dawn
Latin: vesper · English: west, vespers — from PIE *wek'spero-; Polish wieczór, Latin vesper (evening star), English west (where the sun sets) all trace to the same evening root

English: ten days — tydzień literally means 'this day' (in the cycle); the seven-day week came to Europe from Babylon through the Jewish/Roman calendar; Sanskrit saptāha (seven-unit = week) uses the same counting logic
Sanskrit: māsa (मास) · Hindi: mahīnā — from PIE *mēns- (moon/month); miesiąc and Sanskrit māsa are direct cognates; the moon (księżyc) measures months; English month and moon share the same PIE root

cards.example_polish: W tym roku jadę do Polski.
cards.example_english: This year I'm going to Poland.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: ṛtu (ऋतु) · English: right, regulate — from PIE *h₃reǵ- (right/regular); a year as the right/regular cycle; Sanskrit ṛtu (season/proper time) and English regulate (from the same root) share the idea of natural order
Hindi: somwār (सोमवार) — poniedziałek = 'after Sunday' (po + niedziela); Hindi somwār = Moon's day (soma = moon); both languages named Monday after the moon or its relation to Sunday

cards.example_english: I have a meeting on Wednesday.
cards.connection: Hindi: budhwār (बुधवार) — środa = middle (of the week); budhwār = Mercury's day (budh = Mercury/wisdom); English Wednesday = Woden's day; all three named the midweek differently — day of wisdom, middle, or Woden
Sanskrit: pañca (पञ्च) — piątek = fifth day (from pięć = five); Sanskrit pañca-devī (Friday) also counts from five; English Friday = Freya's day; Polish simply counted: the fifth day

cards.example_english: On Saturday I go for a walk.
cards.connection: Hebrew: Shabbat · Hindi: śaniwār — sobota from Hebrew Shabbat (day of rest); Hebrew shabbat spread through Christianity and Islam into Polish; English Saturday = Saturn's day; all named after different sacred concepts

cards.example_english: On Sunday we go to church.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: akarman (no-work day) — niedziela = 'no-work day' (nie = no + działać = to work/act); Sanskrit akarman (non-action day) expresses the same concept; English Sunday = Sun's day

cards.example_english: Yesterday I was at the cinema.
cards.connection: Sanskrit: hyas (ह्यस्) · Hindi: kal (कल) — from PIE *dʰǵʰyes- (yesterday); wczoraj and Sanskrit hyas are direct cognates; English yesterday also traces here; Hindi kal means both yesterday and tomorrow — the day adjacent to today

Sanskrit: śvas (श्वस्) · Hindi: kal (कल) — jutro from PIE *yew-tro (the next dawn); Sanskrit śvas (tomorrow), English tomorrow (to + morrow = toward the next morning); Hindi kal serves for both past and future adjacent days
Sanskrit: vāma (वाम) · Latin: laevus · English: left — from PIE *léwos; Polish lewo, Latin laevus, and Sanskrit vāma (left — also meaning beautiful/contrary) all from the same root

Sanskrit: prāk (प्राक्) · English: right, correct — from PIE *prok'- (forward/right); prawo means both 'right direction' and 'law/right'; English right (direction and correct) perfectly mirrors this dual meaning

Sanskrit: prastha (प्रस्थ) · English: prostrate, first — from PIE *pro-steh₂- (stretched out forward); prosto and Sanskrit prastha (plateau = spread-flat) and English prostrate (stretched forward) share the root
Sanskrit: tad (तद्) · English: this, that, the — from PIE *to- (demonstrative); tutaj, Sanskrit tad, English this/that/the all use the same PIE demonstrative sound to point at things
Sanskrit: tad (तद्) · Hindi: vahān (वहाँ) · English: there, that — same PIE *to- demonstrative as tutaj; tam, there, Sanskrit tad — the pointing finger of language
English: bliss, bless — blisko from Slavic *blizъ (near); English bless (to make near/holy) and bliss (nearness to happiness) distantly relate to the concept of closeness
Sanskrit: dīrgha (दीर्घ) · English: tall, long — from PIE *dl̥H-gʰo-; daleko and Sanskrit dīrgha (long/far) share the concept of extended distance
Sanskrit: dvāra (द्वार) · Hindi: darvāzā — dworzec from dwór (court/yard), from PIE *dʰwer- (door/gateway); the train station as the great gateway; Sanskrit dvāra (door) is a direct cognate
English: flight, flee — lotnisko from lot (flight) from *letět (to fly); English flight and flee from PIE *plewd- (to flow/fly); the airport as the flying-place

Sanskrit: atithi (अतिथि) · Latin: hospes — from PIE *gʰosti- (guest); Polish hotel, English hospital, and Sanskrit atithi (guest, literally 'one without a fixed date') all express the sacred guest-host relationship
Latin: restaurare · English: restore — restauracja from French restaurant (a restorative broth); the original restaurants served bouillon to restore health; English restore shares the same Latin root

cards.example_english: I'll buy it at the market.
cards.connection: Hindi: bāzār (बाज़ार) · Persian: bāzār — bazar is the SAME WORD in Polish and Hindi, both borrowed from Persian bāzār; the Silk Road brought this word to both Poland and India

Sanskrit: para (पर) · English: port, pass — paszport = French passe (to pass) + port (gate/harbor); PIE *pṓr- (crossing/ford); Sanskrit para (beyond/other side), English ford (river crossing) — all about the passage across a boundary
French: billet · English: bill, bulletin — bilet from French billet (small document/seal); English bill and bulletin share the same root; a ticket as a small written authorization

Sanskrit: citi (चिति) · Latin: poena · English: pain, penal — from PIE *kʷey- (payment/value/penalty); cena (price), Latin poena (punishment/fine), English pain and penal — all from the concept of value and what must be paid
